newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president's son faces arrest for bribery.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president's son faces arrest for bribery.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors on Thursday grilled President Kim Young-sam's son over kickbacks, illicit political funds and influence-peddling, and the younger Kim's arrest appeared imminent.
"Prosecutors have secured enough evidence that he violated laws," a prosecution official said shortly after Kim Hyun-chul arrived at the Supreme Public Prosecutor's office.
"We are trying to secure his confession."
Senior prosecutor Shim Je-ryoon told reporters the president's second son, dubbed the "crown prince", admitted accepting money from businessmen but denied taking bribes.
Prosecution sources said Kim Hyun-chul would be arrested soon, probably by Saturday.
Prosecutors said they had established the younger Kim took at least two billion won ($2.2 million) from several companies, while associates managed more than 10 billion won for him.
Opposition parties have alleged most of the money handled by the aides was left over from president Kim's 1992 election campaign, in which the younger Kim played a key role.

"Even if Mr Kim Hyun-chul denies taking bribes we have enough evidence to charge him with criminal offences," said one prosecution official, asking not to be identified. Prosecutors had traced more than 100 bank accounts of Kim Hyun-chul's associates and their relatives.
Shim said investigators ordered former top intelligence officer Kim Ki-sup, an associate of the president's son, to report for questioning on Friday.

Kim Ki-sup would be questioned about a seven billion won fund the prosecution suspected he managed through an executive of the Hansol Group, the country's 16th largest business conglomerate, on behalf of Kim Hyun-chul.
The arrest of the president's son would signal the end of a five-month prosecution probe into a sleaze scandal uncovered by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January under five trillion won in debts.
Eleven people, including three top aides of president Kim, are on trial for their involvement in the Hanbo scandal.
But questions remain about President Kim's role in what has become known as "Hanbogate".
Opposition parties have alleged Kim Hyun-chul pressured banks to give loans to Hanbo as a reward for election donations of up to 90 billion won from Hanbo's founder.
There is mounting public pressure on president Kim to make a full declaration on his campaign financing.
The answers he provides could determine whether Kim lasts until the end of his single term next February, or becomes the ultimate victim of the scandal engulfing his administration.
Illicit slush funds helped land Kim's two immediate predecessors, Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo, in jail.
Kim Young-sam took power on an anti-corruption platform, and his administration spent its early years flushing into the open "black" money hidden during previous corrupt governments.

Yet while the public clamours for answers on whether Kim Young-sam knew that key members of his anti-graft administration were on the take, few voices are calling openly for his resignation or impeachment.
There is a widespread belief the president may genuinely have been kept in ignorance of corruption all around him.
And there are worries that a constitutional crisis, on top of an economic downturn and a string of corporate bankruptcies, may be too much for South Korea's infant democracy to bear.
"The country is going through hard times. I wouldn't want to see more chaos with the president resigning," said Lee Byung-ok, an 81-year-old pastor.
Ordinary South Koreans, however, welcomed legal action against the younger Kim.
"Kim Hyun-chul must pay for his sins, and must be judged by the law," said factory worker Kyung Yoon-duk, 43, echoing a view expressed by a number of others. ($1 = 893 won)
